pages.text: Both brackets hold the same `x`, so one pointer feeds both bars. If two numbers multiply to zero, at least one is zero: if the first is not zero, divide both sides by it, and the second is 0 ÷ the first, which is 0. So the product bar reaches zero only where the `x − 2` or the `x − 5` bar does, at `x = 2` and `x = 5`.

pages.task: Values of `x` that make an equation true are its [[roots]], a different job from a square root. Which are the roots of `(x − 2)(x − 5) = 0`?
pages.why: A product is zero only when at least one of its factors is zero. `x − 2` is zero at `x = 2`, and `x − 5` at `x = 5`. Put each back and you get `0 × −3 = 0` and `3 × 0 = 0`.

pages.text: Set equal to 10, the product is 10 at `x = 0` and `x = 7`, where neither bracket is 10. So `x − 2 = 10` gives a wrong `x = 12`, where the product is 70. Expand first: `x² − 7x + 10 = 10`, so `x² − 7x = 0`, which is `x(x − 7) = 0`.

pages.task: Spot the slip. A worked answer to `x² − 5x = 6` goes `x(x − 5) = 6`, then `x = 6` or `x − 5 = 6`, so `x = 6` or `x = 11`. Which step is wrong?
pages.why: Setting each bracket to 6 works only for a product of 0. Take the 6 across first: `x² − 5x − 6 = 0` factorises to `(x − 6)(x + 1) = 0`, so `x = 6` or `x = −1`. Both check, since `36 − 30 = 6` and `1 + 5 = 6`, but 11 makes 66.

pages.task: In Calculus fundamentals, the volume of the box cut from a 30 cm sheet had slope `12x² − 240x + 900`. Solve `12x² − 240x + 900 = 0`.
pages.why: Every term divides by 12, which is never 0, so `x² − 20x + 75 = 0`, which is `(x − 5)(x − 15) = 0`. So `x = 5` or `x = 15`. Both check: `300 − 1,200 + 900 = 0` and `2,700 − 3,600 + 900 = 0`. At 15 cm the cuts meet and there is no box, so 5 cm is the cut found there.
